description:
Walks a site from a starting page and reports what only a crawl can see: pages sharing a
title or a meta description, internal links that are broken and which page links to
them, pages asking not to be indexed, and how much of the site was reachable at all.

Use it after a site rebuild or a migration, and before a quarterly report — the findings
here are the ones a client never notices and a search engine always does. Use it to
answer "why are these pages competing with each other?", "are there broken links
anywhere on the site?" or "is anything still marked noindex from staging?".

Do not use it to audit one page in depth — that is seo_audit, which reports canonical,
Open Graph, hreflang, images without alt text and the sitemap for a single URL. Do not
use it to check whether a site is up (uptime_check) or to inspect a certificate
(ssl_check). It judges only what is in the HTML, never how a page ranks.

It stays on one origin: https://example.com and https://www.example.com are different
origins and only the one you start from is visited. A starting page that redirects to
another origin, as an apex to www often does, is not followed: the report names where it
went, and the crawl should be run again from there.

robots.txt is read first and obeyed for every URL before it is requested. An unreadable
robots.txt is treated as forbidding everything, per RFC 9309, and the crawl reports that
rather than proceeding.

It costs one request per page, paced at one every half second per host, so 25 pages is
about fifteen seconds. Three budgets bound it — pages, depth, and a two-minute deadline —
and whichever one stopped the crawl is reported along with how many URLs were left
unvisited, because a report that does not say it saw a quarter of the site is worse than
no report.

maxDepth.description: How many links deep from the starting page to follow. Defaults to 3. 0 fetches only the starting page. Three reaches everything a small business site has; past that the page budget is the real bound anyway. Example: 2

maxPages.description: How many pages to fetch. Defaults to 25, at most 100. Every page is one request paced at one every half second, so this is the cost: 25 pages is about fifteen seconds, 100 about a minute. Pages found and not visited are counted and reported. Example: 50

url.description: The page to start from, e.g. "https://example.com/"; a bare host such as "example.com" is tried over https. No user name or password: a URL carrying one is refused. The crawl stays on this URL's origin, so start at the address the site actually serves: https://example.com and https://www.example.com are different origins and only one of them will be visited.

name: site_crawl

broken.description: Internal links the site itself says are broken — an HTTP error status (404, 410, 5xx…), a name that does not resolve, a certificate browsers refuse — with the page each was found on, which is the half of a broken link report that makes it fixable.

reason.description: What went wrong, in plain words.

status.description: The status it answered with, or 0 when nothing did.

url.description: The URL that did not answer usefully.

checkedAt.description: When the crawl ran, ISO 8601 in UTC.

couldNotCheck.description: Internal links that gave no verdict — a timeout, a dropped connection, a response this client would not read, a 429 — which says nothing about whether they work.

reason.description: Why no verdict came back, in plain words.

crawl.description: What the crawl covered, and what it did not.

deepestLevel.description: The furthest depth reached from the starting page.

leftTheOrigin.description: URLs that redirected to another host. They are not recorded as pages of this site and their links are not followed: robots.txt was read for the origin the crawl started on, and it does not speak for anybody else.

notVisited.description: URLs found, allowed, and left unfetched because a budget ran out. Zero means the crawl saw the whole of what it could reach.

pagesFetched.description: How many pages were actually requested and answered.

skippedByRobots.description: URLs found and not requested because robots.txt forbids this crawler.

stoppedBecause.description: Why the crawl ended. "nothing left to visit" means it finished; anything else means the site is larger than what was looked at.

duplicates.description: What only a crawl can see. One page cannot tell you that its title is the same as forty others', and that is the commonest reason a site's pages compete with each other in search results.

descriptions.description: Meta descriptions used by more than one page.

titles.description: Titles used by more than one page, with the pages using them.

items.description: One actionable observation about the target.

code.description: Stable identifier for this kind of observation, e.g. "cert_expires_soon".

message.description: One sentence explaining the observation in plain words.

severity.description: How much attention this needs. "critical" means act now; "warning" means act this month; "unknown" means the check could not establish the fact, which is not the same as it being fine.

origin.description: The origin it stayed on, e.g. "https://example.com".

pages.description: Every page fetched, in the order they were visited.

canonical.description: The canonical URL the page declares, resolved.

depth.description: How many links from the starting page this was found at. 0 is it.

h1Count.description: How many <h1> elements the page has. One is the healthy answer.

isHtml.description: Whether it was served as HTML and could be read at all.

linkedFrom.description: The page it was found on. Null for the starting page.

noindex.description: Whether a robots meta tag asks search engines not to index this page.

requestedUrl.description: The URL that was requested, which differs from "url" when it redirected.

status.description: HTTP status of the final response.

title.description: The <title>, or null when there is none.

url.description: The page, as it finally answered — after any redirect.

severity.description: How much attention this needs. "critical" means act now; "warning" means act this month; "unknown" means the check could not establish the fact, which is not the same as it being fine.

startUrl.description: The URL the crawl was asked to start from.

title: Technical SEO across a site
